[1269] A defense for our time

[1270] Network-based organization opens up new possibilities, and at the same time challenges traditional concepts, command relationships, management forms and organization

[1271] The network-based Armed Forces therefore requires both conceptual and organizational renewal

[1272] After the Cold War, the Armed Forces have been significantly reduced in the number of units and departments

[1273] At the same time, combat power and operational ability to solve tasks have increased

[1274] This is due to the continuous modernization and systematic application of new, advanced technology in the Armed Forces organization and in military operations

[1275] The development has several consequences

[1276] Firstly, newer weapons systems can perform more tasks than older ones, which means that they can fully or partially replace several older systems or their functions and roles

[1277] Secondly, each individual platform is often so efficient that it is no longer necessary to have the same number of units

[1278] A smaller number of platforms can often not only handle the same tasks, but also solve new ones

[1279] A reduction in volume therefore does not mean that the Armed Forces are weakened – often the operational effect can not only be maintained, but also strengthened, even if the number of platforms and personnel is reduced

[1280] At the same time, there is a limit to how low the number of units can be before the capacity loses its relevance

[1281] While technological developments contribute to strengthening the Armed Forces' operational capabilities, they also affect cost developments

[1282] Military equipment often has a price increase that differs from the general price increase

[1283] This applies to both the investment itself and the costs from a life-cycle perspective

[1284] This is due not least to the increase in capacity of the equipment from one generation to the next

[1285] The rise in prices for military materiel and equipment is creating pressure on the Armed Forces' finances

[1286] At a time of generally reduced defense appropriations in many European countries, this is a significant challenge for defense planning

[1287] Investments in new systems must balance the need for advanced and expensive cutting-edge technology and cheaper equipment that maintains a modest but adequate standard

[1288] In certain crucial areas, the Armed Forces must continue to acquire high-tech equipment to meet defense and security policy needs

[1289] This is particularly true with regard to critical capabilities such as frigates, combat aircraft with precision weapons and certain types of military equipment, where the Armed Forces must continue to invest in "state of the art" technology

[1290] These are often systems that are at the forefront of technological development and as such will be necessary to maintain operational capability, interoperability with allies and personnel safety

[1291] For other areas that are less critical, the Armed Forces must make greater use of fully developed technological material

[1292] Not least, the technological increase in cost will mean that the Armed Forces will have to invest more in standardized technology ("off-the-shelf goods

[1293] For many purposes, this type of technology, already developed for civilian society, will be sufficient for the Armed Forces

[1294] Network-based defense (NBD) is about how military operations can be carried out by linking units and departments from all branches of defense in networks using information technology

[1295] Instead of focusing on what the individual platforms (for example, aircraft or vessels) can do individually, NbF emphasizes creating a seamless community of different platforms that can collaborate smoothly and effectively based on the fact that they all have access to a common situational picture and can communicate quickly and effectively with each other

[1296] This makes it possible to link different military functions in a flexible manner, which allows for increased speed in the exercise of command and control, increased tempo and precision in operations, and increased combat and survivability

[1297] The overall effect of different platforms becomes much greater if they can operate in networks

[1298] Great emphasis is placed on integrating the Norwegian Defence Force's new capabilities into a comprehensive network

[1299] The frigates, coastal corvettes, F-35 fighter jets, NH 90 helicopters, the Army's command posts and combat vehicles, as well as the command structure, must be able to operate in networks and complement each other

[1300] In addition, great emphasis is placed on developing the organization, processes and procedures, and understanding the opportunities that NBF offers

[1301] A central element in NbF is the dissemination and management of information

[1302] This requires human resources with the right expertise

[1303] Therefore, the introduction of new technology and the development of expertise, culture and organization are important prerequisites for achieving the desired effect of network-based defense

[1304] The Norwegian Armed Forces shall develop its network-based capabilities in line with developments in NATO and society at large, so that the Norwegian Armed Forces can cooperate effectively within a joint operational framework, both nationally and within NATO

[1305] Cooperation within NATO therefore has a significant influence on the development of the NbF concept

[1306] A defense for our time

[1307] At the same time, technology has its limitations

[1308] New, advanced technology alone cannot solve all the challenges for the Armed Forces

[1309] One system may be very relevant in one type of scenario, and to a lesser extent in another

[1310] For example, the ability to deliver long-range precision fire would be necessary in a high-intensity conflict, but would not be as relevant in a peacekeeping operation

[1311] Furthermore, lightly equipped personnel on the ground may be relevant in one type of conflict, but not in another

[1312] In a scenario-robust defense, however, it is crucial to have access to a broad range of instruments, where high technology and competent personnel are important elements

[1313] Furthermore, the introduction of new technology places great demands on the personnel who will use the systems, and on management and the ability to interact in networks

[1314] In order to master and utilize the systems in the best possible way, personnel must have the necessary expertise, which must be reflected in the Armed Forces' education and recruitment

[1315] Cost developments and tight financial constraints make it necessary to consider other types of instruments for acquiring expensive equipment as a supplement to traditional purchases

[1316] As part of this, the Armed Forces will, among other things, consider acquiring used equipment to a greater extent, as well as equipment that has become available due to canceled orders in related countries

[1317] Increased need for multinational capability and materiel cooperation The cost development within military technology, combined with tight financial constraints, makes it necessary to seek multinational cooperation and integration in connection with the development, acquisition, operation and maintenance of defence materiel

[1318] Establishing new or continuing existing, advanced and costly capabilities can in many cases only be done in a multinational framework

[1319] The difficult economic situation among many of our allies and partners is not the only driving force behind this development

[1320] Future military challenges will, to an even greater extent than before, require the Armed Forces to be flexible and adaptable

[1321] Broad participation in military operations is also a driving force for enhanced, structured multinational cooperation

[1322] Developments are increasingly moving in the direction of cooperation across alliance and organizational affiliations

[1323] The operations within the framework of ISAF in Afghanistan fully demonstrate that allies and partners cooperate closely and in an integrated manner

[1324] Multinational force cooperation is often practiced at a lower tactical level than previously

[1325] This creates new needs for equality in procedures, training and equipment, among other things

[1326] Such multinational cooperation can also be important in supporting national force contributions

[1327] Partners who have the same weapons systems and are similarly organized find it easier to establish cost-saving cooperation

[1328] In other words, system similarity will create greater opportunities to extract benefits through cooperation within both force production, logistics and operational activities

[1329] It is natural that it takes time to establish system equality, but the goal should always be clear

[1330] The Government further believes that the basis for operational cooperation can be strengthened through early and forward-looking planning

[1331] Experience from previous and ongoing operations must play an important role in the design of new solutions and mechanisms that can improve the ability for joint deployments and cooperation in operations

[1332] The Armed Forces' participation in multinational capability cooperation is discussed in more detail in chapter

[1333] Vulnerabilities in the digital space

[1334] The digital space is used to create, store and share important information

[1335] Networked information and communication systems (ICT) support critical management and control functions in most sectors of society

[1336] Failures in these systems create vulnerability and can occur as a result of technical and human error, but also as a result of deliberate attacks

[1337] The threat to society's ICT systems as a result of such attacks is great and increasing, and the methods are becoming increasingly professional and sophisticated

[1338] In particular, the number of serious, targeted attempts at espionage and sabotage against public and private enterprises has increased in recent years

[1339] Digital attacks are complex and challenging to deal with

[1340] If such attacks cause critical societal functions to collapse for an extended period, the consequences could be major

[1341] Digital attacks can, for example, cause power supply failures, disruptions in the financial system, or the Norwegian Armed Forces' command and control systems to be affected

[1342] Due to technical dependence, failure in one system will quickly have ripple effects in other systems, both in one's own and other sectors of society, and across national borders

[1343] Two factors in particular make attacks in the digital space challenging

[1344] Firstly, during and after attacks it can be difficult to determine with certainty

[1345] who the attacker is, since there are great opportunities to hide the sender's identity

[1346] Secondly, it can be difficult to confirm the nature of the attack, that is, whether the purpose is financial gain or destruction

[1347] This is due, among other things, to the fact that an attacker 2011–2012 Prop

[1348] A defence for our time can be present in an ICT system for a long time before a planned attack, which helps make it difficult to put the attack into the correct context

[1349] Environmental developments and consequences for the Armed Forces

[1350] The world faces major environmental and climate challenges

[1351] A major challenge is the lack of international agreement on joint binding agreements to solve the problems

[1352] Norway has set itself the goal of being a pioneer in the work towards sustainable development

[1353] The defense sector follows the national environmental policy and ensures environmental responsibility within its own sector, and in collaboration with civil society where appropriate

[1354] Many environmental problems can be solved locally, and here the defense sector is an important societal actor

[1355] We are already seeing the consequences of a changing climate

[1356] Rising temperatures, increased precipitation, sea levels and flooding, more frequent landslides and strong winds are all climate changes that directly affect the Armed Forces' activities

[1357] At the same time, the Armed Forces have their own responsibility to find good solutions and effective means to reduce their own impact on the environment

[1358] The defense's environmental challenges are particularly related to the use of materiel, training and exercises that cause environmental damage to our surroundings

[1359] But chemicals that are hazardous to health and the environment also pose a major challenge for the Defense Forces

[1360] These are substances that break down slowly in nature and accumulate in food chains

[1361] Environmental toxins are a serious threat to the diversity of nature and also pose a health risk to those who work directly with such substances

[1362] The defense sector's environmental responsibility requires holistic thinking in which measures and instruments are put into context and adapted to specific environmental challenges

[1363] The Armed Forces must maintain expertise in environmental issues and ensure that new knowledge is safeguarded and that new requirements and measures are taken into account in defense planning, both with regard to materiel, maintenance, new acquisitions, exercises, training and operations

[1364] Climate change is affecting the Armed Forces' operational environment in the form of, among other things, more extreme weather, and the challenge for the Armed Forces therefore also consists of adapting its own structure and activities to changing environments

[1365] The Armed Forces' activities from an environmental perspective

[1366] The Armed Forces fulfill one of our most important societal tasks related to the country's security

[1367] To solve this task, personnel must train, which requires active use of space both in the air, at sea and on land

[1368] A large part of the training causes various forms of strain on nature and the local environment, such as land occupation, noise and pollution

[1369] The defense sector has a responsibility to take environmental considerations into account when planning and carrying out activities

[1370] One measure could be to use alternative forms of training that do not put as much strain on the environment

[1371] For example, costly and environmentally damaging training can be reduced by using simulators in education

[1372] The use of simulators can reduce environmental impacts such as emissions of greenhouse gases, noise, chemicals hazardous to health and the environment, and reduce terrain damage

[1373] At the same time, it must be emphasized that the Armed Forces are a legitimate user of areas for training purposes, and that pressures cannot be completely avoided

[1374] The goal must be to reduce these impacts as much as possible through environmentally conscious planning and execution of such activities

[1375] The defense sector's environmental management system should contribute to ensuring that environmental and social responsibility is given weight in all planning and decision-making processes

[1376] This also means that the Armed Forces must emphasize safeguarding indigenous interests in dialogue with indigenous organizations on affected matters

[1377] Central to the environmental management system is a commitment to continuous improvement of the Armed Forces' environmental impact

[1378] Environmental work should be based on the precautionary principle, the polluter pays principle and the principle of total burden, which means that emphasis should be placed on the sum of the impacts on the natural environment, cf. the Natural Diversity Act

[1379] Environmental protection work in the defense sector includes both prevention of pollution and cleanup of past pollution

[1380] The external environment must be taken into account in all parts of the business, in Norway and in international operations

[1381] This means that, as far as possible, the same strict environmental protection considerations should be applied during international operations

[1382] The defense sector's businesses should be drivers in demanding goods and services that satisfy environmental and social responsibility requirements

[1383] The defense sector must have a good overview and control of its activities, including input factors and products that can lead to negative environmental impacts

[1384] The defense sector has established its own environmental database that will be used to improve knowledge of environmental conditions, as a basis for environmentally effective improvement measures and as a source for annual environmental reporting

[1385] An environmental report and an environmental account are prepared annually, describing the sector's environmental challenges with a discussion of implemented and planned measures

[1386] A defense for our time

[1387] Biodiversity and pollution

[1388] The expertise regarding biological diversity in the Armed Forces' shooting and training ranges and other managed areas must be maintained, and consideration for biodiversity must be given importance in the use and management of the managed areas, cf. the Biodiversity Act, §

[1389] The defense sector must have knowledge about the occurrence of cultural heritage and cultural environments in the exercise and operational areas

[1390] It is a national goal that cultural heritage and cultural environments should be managed and preserved as usable resources, and as a basis for knowledge, experiences and value creation

[1391] Cultural heritage must be secured for current and future generations

[1392] The defense sector shall follow up on national targets for chemicals hazardous to health and the environment, and shall continuously reduce emissions and use of chemicals that pose a threat to health and the environment with the goal of stopping emissions

[1393] The spread of environmental toxins from contaminated soil must be stopped or significantly reduced

[1394] The Armed Forces will follow up on the phase-out target for environmental toxins and for substances on the list of prioritized environmental toxins

[1395] The Armed Forces will also follow up on goals to minimize risks from the release and use of other chemicals

[1396] Seabeds contaminated by the defense sector's past activities should not pose a risk of serious pollution problems

[1397] The seabed must be remediated, if necessary, to stop the spread of environmental toxins to water bodies and reduce the risk of absorption by organisms

[1398] The sector's businesses must carry out source separation of all categories of waste and handle it so that waste resources can be reused or recycled

[1399] The defense sector must significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the use of fossil energy for heating by

[1400] Priority measures to reduce emissions to the air, including in urban areas, will be implemented continuously

[1401] Purchased energy for real estate construction and facilities (EBA) shall be reduced by 30 percent in 2016 measured in relation to

[1402] A plan shall be established with annual targets for greenhouse gas emissions and for purchased energy specified for each energy carrier

[1403] Climate accounting will soon be established for all managed properties based on the international standard for climate accounting, the Greenhouse Gas Protocol

[1404] Complete renovation of buildings must be based on the energy requirements in building regulations

[1405] Defence Building must ensure that existing and new ESA and infrastructure are adapted to changing climate conditions with regard to wind, precipitation, landslides and humidity

[1406] Environmental considerations related to force production, exercises and operational activities The Armed Forces' exercises must be designed so that there are as few negative effects on the environment as possible

[1407] Consideration for preserving the environment must be an integrated part of all exercise planning

[1408] For all activities outside of its own firing and training ranges, the Armed Forces have a special responsibility regarding the prevention of and compensation for environmental damage

[1409] From a historical perspective, the Armed Forces are responsible for significant pollution, not least in older firing ranges

[1410] This is partly due to a lack of knowledge and awareness of environmental damage in the past, and partly a perception that the role of the Armed Forces in safeguarding national security and independence meant that environmental considerations had to take precedence anyway

[1411] Today, the level of knowledge and attitudes have changed, and the defense sector takes responsibility for cleanup where necessary

[1412] Therefore, the defense sector will continue its work on clearing explosives and environmental remediation of firing and training ranges and other land, so that decommissioned properties can be disposed of for civilian purposes

[1413] Environmental conditions at the local level must be taken into account when operating abroad

[1414] Local operations must be arranged for the most resource- and environmentally friendly management possible

[1415] The limits of what water bodies can withstand in terms of consumption and load are critical in many areas

[1416] Arrangements must be made to minimize water use and to ensure that handling of used water causes the least possible damage to local conditions

[1417] The need for electricity during operations abroad is often met by the use of diesel generators

[1418] Such electricity production results in a large consumption of diesel, local and global emissions and is a source of local pollution

[1419] Furthermore, procuring diesel can pose a significant logistical challenge that entails a risk of pollution

[1420] Resources and environmentally friendly production and use of energy must be actively facilitated, and more future-oriented and environmentally friendly forms of energy must be sought

[1421] A defense for our time

[1422] Implications for the application and design of the Armed Forces

[1423] The societal trends described here set the guidelines and premises for the further development and organization of the Armed Forces

[1424] – Factors such as increased competition for labor, centralization, dual-career families and higher requirements for competence present the Armed Forces with a significant challenge when it comes to securing access to personnel to maintain and maintain competence

[1425] The Armed Forces must appear as an attractive workplace when recruiting and training personnel, and the Armed Forces must have the ability to look after the personnel and their loved ones. – The Armed Forces must continue to highlight its position in society as a recognized, diverse, high-tech and attractive workplace

[1426] – It is important that a holistic understanding and broad competence are maintained in parallel with the increasing need for specialized competence

[1427] – The introduction of new technology places great demands on the personnel who will use the systems, and on management and the ability to interact in networks

[1428] In order to master and utilize the systems in the best possible way, personnel must have the necessary competence, which should be reflected in recruitment, selection and education

[1429] This also applies to conscripts, especially those serving their first term

[1430] – Increased interdependence and an increasingly blurred distinction between civilian and military actors in operations place great demands on orderliness and clarity in terms of roles and responsibilities

[1431] This requires thorough consideration of legal and ethical issues, among other things

[1432] In the future, the Armed Forces will increasingly be able to meet such challenges in connection with international operations. – The increasing complexity of the interaction between military and civilian actors places great demands on education and awareness among personnel, especially in management functions

[1433] This requires a values-based approach where competence, reflection and maturity are emphasized in relation to ethical issues both within the Armed Forces and in interaction with other actors

[1434] – The challenges resulting from, among other things, the global economic crisis and the cost development of defense materiel make it necessary to cooperate with other countries to reduce costs and to maintain and further develop the Armed Forces' operational capability

[1435] Multinational cooperation on the development, acquisition, operation and maintenance of materiel will be central to the Armed Forces in the years ahead

[1436] Multinational cooperation in these and other areas will be a strategy to avoid or reduce the need for further cuts to the defense structure, as well as ensure access to necessary capabilities. – Among Norway's allies, defense budgets are being reduced at the same time as investment and operating costs are increasing

[1437] This development could have consequences for NATO in the long term

[1438] Increased need for cost sharing and economies of scale will entail more multinational cooperation

[1439] This allows Norway to gain better access to advanced, high-capacity materiel that the Norwegian Defense Forces could not have operated alone

[1440] On the other hand, this development could lead to our allies having a reduced ability to support Norway in a crisis or war situation

[1441] Norway may be faced with expectations to take on greater responsibility – both in NATO and at home. The Armed Forces must take into account the increasing vulnerability to threats to information and communication infrastructure and general attacks in the digital space, which a high-tech and network-based defense entails

[1442] There is therefore a need to strengthen further work to define and further develop the Armed Forces' activities in the digital space

[1443] The digital space is already an important battle arena, and it is important that the further modernization of the Armed Forces takes into account the ability to conduct both defensive and offensive operations in this field

[1444] – The Armed Forces' focus on network-based defense involves increased use of information technology

[1445] The Ministry of Defence has decided to initiate work to develop guidelines that will define the defence sector's work within the digital space, and establish responsibilities, tasks and authorities for the ministry and subordinate agencies. – In order to reduce the environmental consequences of the Defence's activities at home and abroad, environmental aspects must be an integrated part of defence planning. – For the Defence, the environmental challenge is twofold

[1446] It primarily consists of measures to reduce the negative environmental consequences of our own operations, but it also includes the necessary adaptation of our own expertise, structure and operations to safeguard our operations in environments that are changing due to climate change

[1447] A defense for our time Defense policy framework and guidelines

[1448] The defence policy defines the framework, guidelines and priorities for the further development of the Defence

[1449] Based on security policy developments and other relevant developments, the defense policy describes why we have a defense force, what the Armed Forces should do and how the tasks should be solved

[1450] This chapter begins with a description of defense policy goals

[1451] The Armed Forces' tasks are then specified with their level of ambition

[1452] Furthermore, key framework factors related to total defence, preparedness and planning, exercises and training, protection against weapons of mass destruction, activities in the digital space and multinational cooperation are described

[1453] The chapter culminates in a set of fundamental principles for the organization of the Armed Forces

[1454] The next part of the proposition describes how the defense sector's structure, capacities and expertise will be developed to follow up on these guidelines

[1455] The security policy developments described in Chapter 3 indicate that there is still a need to further develop a response defence that can meet complex security challenges to Norwegian national and societal security

[1456] The armed forces must be able to handle a wide range of missions at home as well as abroad

[1457] In recent years, the Armed Forces have contributed to a number of operations that have presented unexpected and demanding challenges, including the deployment of Norwegian frigates and surveillance aircraft in the fight against piracy in the Gulf of Aden, participation with Norwegian fighter jets in the air military operation over Libya, a continued commitment in Afghanistan and the Armed Forces' assistance in connection with the terrorist acts of July

[1458] This emphasizes the need for a defense that is flexible, robust and capable of dealing with many different scenarios

[1459] Norway must have a defense force that is capable of delivering customized contributions within a broad spectrum of missions, both planned and unforeseen, within and beyond the country's borders, in cooperation with allies, partners or civilian actors

[1460] In a changing and unpredictable world, it is crucial that the Armed Forces be developed as a preventive instrument

[1461] The Armed Forces, together with allied capabilities, shall represent a war-preventing threshold

[1462] Such a threshold means that Norway, within the framework of NATO, has relevant means of power that can counteract pressure, aggression or attacks

[1463] Alliance membership remains the cornerstone of Norwegian security and defense policy

[1464] Norway's defense is a contribution to NATO's overall stabilizing and conflict prevention capability

[1465] The importance of the Armed Forces as a warpreventing threshold means that the Armed Forces have several parallel functions

[1466] On the one hand, the Armed Forces will contribute continuously to operations – at home in the form of presence, border guarding, fisheries supervision and other routine missions, and abroad in the form of contributions to international operations

[1467] On the other hand, the Armed Forces have a threshold function, where the purpose is not necessarily to use the capacities in ongoing operations, but to highlight a capability that will cause others to refrain from actions that could trigger the active use of Norwegian and allied military power

[1468] Defence policy goals

[1469] The Government believes that the main content of the existing defence policy objectives should be continued

[1470] The defense policy goals reflect that the Armed Forces, within its area of responsibility and in cooperation with other national authorities where this is natural, shall contribute to fulfilling these goals: – Alone and together with allies, secure Norwegian sovereignty, Norwegian rights, interests and values, and preserve Norwegian freedom of action against military and other pressure

[1471] – Through participation in international peace operations with an unambiguous anchoring in the UN Charter and international defense cooperation, contribute to peace, stability, enforcement of international law and respect for human rights, and prevent the use of force by states and non-state actors against Norwegian and international security. – Together with allies, contribute to the collective defense of Norway and other allies in accordance with our alliance commitments, and to meet various types of 2011–2012 Prop

[1472] A defense for our time: attacks and threats to ensure Norwegian and collective security. – Contribute to safeguarding Norwegian societal security, saving lives and limiting the consequences of accidents, disasters, attacks and threats from state and non-state actors

[1473] In order to provide guidance in the specific design of the Armed Forces' structure and activities, the defence policy objectives have been operationalised

[1474] This is done through the Armed Forces' tasks and associated level of ambition, as well as in the basic principles for the organisation of the Armed Forces (cf. 5.3 and 5.8 below

[1475] The tasks of the Armed Forces

[1476] The tasks of the Armed Forces and the associated level of ambition are an operationalization of the security and defense policy goals

[1477] The tasks also constitute the concrete framework for designing the Norwegian Defence's activities, capacities, structure and expertise

[1478] The Government has found a need to revise and update the tasks of the Armed Forces in light of security policy developments and other framework factors

[1479] The purpose of the audit is to clarify

[1480] The basic functions of the Armed Forces

[1481] The main content of the tasks is continued from the St. prop

[1482] No. 48 (2007–

[1483] However, some clarifications have been made in the use of terms

[1484] In addition, the Defence Force's preventive function has been included in the task set

[1485] The tasks of the Armed Forces are the government's overall mandate to the Armed Forces

[1486] The structure and operational capacities of the Armed Forces must be developed to be able to carry out missions within their framework

[1487] The tasks are therefore accompanied by guidelines for how the tasks should be used as a basis for the Armed Forces' planning

[1488] It states which of the tasks will primarily be solved with national resources and which must be solved in collaboration with the alliance and possibly others

[1489] Each of the tasks is also accompanied by a text that describes the content of the task and indicates the level of ambition

[1490] It is the entirety of these frameworks and guidelines that constitute the tasks of the Armed Forces

[1491] The tasks of the Armed Forces can be summarized under the following headings

[1492] To constitute a war-preventing threshold based on NATO membership To defend Norway and allies against serious threats, attacks and attacks, within the framework of NATO's collective defence To avert and handle incidents and security policy crises with national resources, including facilitating allied engagement if necessary To ensure a national basis for decision-making through timely monitoring

[1493] and intelligence Asserted Norwegian sovereignty and sovereign rights

[1494] Maintain the exercise of authority in defined areas Participate in multinational crisis management, including peace-support operations Contribute to international cooperation in the area of defence and security policy Contribute to the maintenance of societal security and other key societal tasks 5.3.1 General guidelines for the tasks The following sets out guidelines that shall form the basis for the tasks of the Armed Forces

[1495] National tasks and allied cooperation tasks

[1496] Some of the Armed Forces' tasks originate from responsibilities and interests that must be considered national and that are linked to Norway and its surrounding areas

[1497] These tasks must be able to be solved with national resources, and initially without any particular degree of ongoing allied involvement

[1498] Tasks 3–6 are all tasks that fall under this category

[1499] Other tasks must be solved in cooperation with others, and primarily with our allies in NATO

[1500] This applies to the central and demanding tasks related to war prevention and defense of Norway and NATO

[1501] This also applies to contributions to peace-supporting and stabilising efforts in the form of international operations, where Norway will make contributions within multilateral frameworks

[1502] Tasks 1, 2 and 7 are included in this category

[1503] Task 8, contributions to international cooperation, cannot initially be divided unambiguously into the categories of national or cooperative tasks

[1504] The task is most often linked to cooperation with allies, but can also encompass purely bilateral assistance

[1505] Task 9, safeguarding social security and other central societal tasks, is essentially a national task

[1506] It will usually include nationally managed situations on one's own territory, but may require cooperation and assistance across national borders, both in relation to allies and others

[1507] A defense for our time

[1508] Dimensioning the Armed Forces depends on which capacities or structural elements the Armed Forces need, and how each capacity should be dimensioned and organized

[1509] Since several tasks require the same military capabilities, the capacity to solve several tasks in parallel is important in this assessment

[1510] Basically, the main elements of the Defence structure are dimensioned to solve tasks 1–

[1511] At the same time, support for civil society must be included in the assessment of the organization and dimensioning of the individual capacities in the Defence Forces

[1512] This is relevant, among other things, when designing dedicated missions, emergency preparedness orders, localization, requirements for training, exercises and practice, as well as the ability to collaborate with actors outside the defense sector

[1513] Task

[1514] Establish a war-prevention threshold based on NATO membership. The purpose of a war-prevention threshold is to ensure that a potential aggressor refrains from using military force against Norway

[1515] The Armed Forces must have the ability to react immediately, effectively and with relevant means if Norway is exposed to pressure, threats or attacks, and have the ability to cooperate with allied forces within the framework of NATO's collective defence

[1516] The ability to handle military challenges should help prevent them from arising

[1517] The foundation of the war-preventing threshold is NATO membership

[1518] Since its establishment, NATO's primary purpose has been to prevent war by having a deterrent capability to fight it if necessary

[1519] It follows from this that a war-preventing threshold does not require Norway alone to be able to repel a comprehensive attack, but to be able to engage an attacker and facilitate allied assistance

[1520] The key point is that the Armed Forces contribute to ensuring that NATO's preventive threshold appears credible in our immediate areas

[1521] It can be assumed that any use of military force against Norway will have limited objectives related to pressuring Norway to change policy or give up rights in specific areas

[1522] Such use of military force will usually be based on limited, rapid and targeted operations, where the intention is to achieve the objectives before Norway and the alliance have had time to deploy effective countermeasures

[1523] An effective war prevention threshold should show that such attacks against Norway would be so risky and have such high costs that it does not appear to be a realistic alternative

[1524] To contribute to a credible allied preventive threshold, the Norwegian Armed Forces must have high quality, combat power, reaction capability, as well as the ability to build up forces and deploy

[1525] The defense must be able to immediately meet challenges throughout Norway's area of interest that must be handled nationally, be able to facilitate allied engagement if necessary, and have the ability to operate effectively and integrated with allied forces

[1526] The Norwegian contribution to conflict prevention in our immediate areas is not primarily made up of individual capacities, but of the Armed Forces' overall capabilities

[1527] The armed forces must therefore have a balanced and adaptable structure with sufficient breadth to be able to meet various forms of pressure and aggression

[1528] Certain capabilities are nevertheless particularly central from a deterrence perspective – for example submarines and a modern combat aircraft

[1529] The armed forces must also have the ability to carry out missions that require the involvement of the entire structure in joint operations, which requires effective command and control systems and adapted operational logistics

[1530] A threshold is given increased credibility through activity that demonstrates military capability in practice

[1531] The Armed Forces must conduct regular exercises with allies to confirm the Armed Forces' ability to participate in complex integrated operations

[1532] The armed forces must also conduct regular training throughout the Norwegian area of interest

[1533] A threshold is also made visible through regular presence

[1534] This contributes to stability and predictability in our local areas

[1535] Defend Norway and allies against serious threats, attacks and attacks, within the framework of NATO's collective defense. The Armed Forces shall defend Norway against external aggression that threatens national security

[1536] Defense of Norway and allies will take place under the auspices of NATO

[1537] The Defence Forces, together with our allies, shall contribute to handling threats, attacks and attacks against Norway and other parts of NATO that are covered by Articles 5 and 6 of the Atlantic Treaty, and meet them in a credible manner

[1538] This includes all types of attacks and threats from both state and non-state actors that cause or threaten to cause such extensive damage that it is appropriate for NATO to implement collective defense measures

[1539] A credible Norwegian contribution to the defense of our own and allied territory is crucial for our influence on NATO's plans and operations

[1540] A defense for our time Defense of Norwegian territory against serious threats, attacks and attacks will be carried out as integrated allied joint operations, where Norwegian forces are part of a broad allied effort

[1541] In such operations, the ability to cooperate and interoperability with allies will be crucial

[1542] This entails quality requirements for both personnel and materials

[1543] The collective defense obligation is mutual

[1544] The defence must therefore also be able to make relevant contributions to the defence of other allies

[1545] The requirements placed on Norwegian military forces in the defense of Norway are broadly the same as those for participation in collective defense in other parts of NATO

[1546] Norway must make a reasonable contribution to NATO's overall level of ambition, with military capabilities that have sufficient quality, responsiveness and endurance to cooperate with allied forces

[1547] Norway will participate continuously and substantially in both NATO's standing response forces, such as NATO

[1548] Response Force (NRF) and the standing maritime forces, as well as in NATO's staff and command structure

[1574] Ensuring a national decision-making basis through timely surveillance and intelligence The main goal of the Armed Forces' surveillance and intelligence activities is to provide a comprehensive situational picture, as a contribution to the best possible decision-making basis for political authorities and the Armed Forces' operational leadership

[1668] Total defence, preparedness, exercises and training Total defence and the Armed Forces' support to civil society

[1669] Total defence shall ensure that society's overall resources, both civilian and military, are used in the best possible way in crisis management in war and peace

[1670] When the total defence concept was first developed in the post-World War II era, the concept primarily encompassed civilian support for the Armed Forces in times of crisis and war

[1671] Arrangements and mechanisms that have been established over time within the total defence are cornerstones in safeguarding Norwegian national and societal security

[1672] In recent years, the concept has been expanded and modernized so that it now places greater emphasis on mutual support and cooperation between the Armed Forces and civil society across the entire crisis spectrum, from peace via security policy crises to war

[1673] The Armed Forces have always contributed support to civil society, but in recent years this has been emphasized much more strongly as an integrated part of the total defense concept

[1674] A defense for our time The actions of July 22, 2011 clearly highlighted the need for the Armed Forces to be prepared to provide such assistance

[1675] The Storting was notified that there would be a review and update of the civil-military cooperation arrangements and mechanisms within the framework of total defence

[1676] In 2010, a working group presented a report that showed that most civil-military cooperation arrangements are still largely adequate for the challenges Norway faces today

[1677] The weaknesses that were uncovered mainly affect arrangements related to civil society's preparedness for support to the Armed Forces in the event of security-political crises and war

[1678] These are arrangements that have changed little since the Cold War

[1679] From an overall preparedness perspective, it is very important that this dimension is also addressed in a satisfactory manner

[1680] The weaknesses that were uncovered particularly affect the Armed Forces' takeover of the management of individual civilian actors in a security crisis/war, needs and roles related to wartime relocation and evacuation of the civilian population, coordination forums and crisis management bodies within the total defense, as well as graded liaison and communication in the civilian part of the total defense

[1681] The government has initiated work to ensure that necessary updates are implemented

[1682] The work should be completed by the end of As part of this work, the defense sector will clarify its needs in relation to the need for support from civil society

[1683] The main principle will continue to be that civilian support to the Armed Forces, to the greatest extent possible, and where time permits, is based on commercial arrangements and cooperation with the civilian sector through delivery and contingency agreements

[1684] In the event of a major or prolonged security crisis, it may nevertheless be necessary to apply emergency legislation to ensure the necessary support for the Defence Forces

[1685] The armed forces must, in collaboration with civilian actors, develop routines for such support

[1686] As part of this, the use of relevant legal bases and cooperation/preparedness arrangements established to ensure society's access to goods and services is considered, if necessary

[1687] The armed forces' assistance to civil society is normally a supplement to the crisis management of civilian authorities

[1688] The primary tasks of the Armed Forces are to assert Norway's sovereignty and defend the country against external attacks (state security), while civilian authorities have the primary responsibility for safeguarding public security

[1753] Securing important objects (for example buildings, facilities, installations and areas) against security threats can be divided into three different main categories or regimes

[1754] Firstly, property owners themselves have a responsibility for preventive safety, that is, passive safety measures

[1755] This responsibility is based on the Security Act and the Object Security Regulations

[1756] NSM is the supervisory authority under the Security Act and regulations

[1757] Within a number of sectors, preventive object security is also authorized by sectoral legislation

[1758] This applies, for example, to ports, power supplies and airports

[1759] In many cases, sectoral legislation is based on international regulations regarding such protection

[1760] Secondly, the police are responsible for securing objects against crime

[1761] In contrast to the passive and preventive security of property owners, police security consists of offensive measures and, if necessary, the use of force to prevent or limit attacks on properties

[1762] The legal basis for this protection is the Police Act, the Criminal Procedure Act, as well as regulations and internal agency regulations

[1763] The police's responsibilities and tasks related to securing facilities do not, in principle, change during crises or armed conflict

[1764] The Armed Forces may, in accordance with the assistance instructions, provide assistance to the police in securing objects

[1765] The Armed Forces also have, as a military police authority (cf. the law on this matter), the authority to secure military objects in collaboration with the police, who can take over the security

[1766] Thirdly, the Armed Forces are responsible for securing facilities through the use of security forces as military defense against an armed attack against the realm

[1767] This will take the form of military protection through offensive security measures for objects that are of crucial importance for the defense capability and military defense and that can be defined as military objectives under the international law of war

[1768] The Armed Forces' authority to provide security will automatically come into effect when a military threat exists in accordance with the terms of international law

[1769] Implementation of military facility security therefore does not need to be dependent on agreements between the Armed Forces and the police, requests for assistance from the police, or similar

[1770] The Armed Forces' facility security is further regulated in the Chief of Defence's Key Points Directive

[1771] In many cases, the Home Guard will be the Armed Forces' most important resource both for assistance to the police's object security and for the Armed Forces' independent responsibility for object security

[1793] Exercise and training The Armed Forces' exercise and training activities encompass a broad spectrum of activities at different levels, and must take into account several considerations

[1794] Exercise and training include everything from training in various individual basic military skills to the ability to operate in large units together with forces from other nations

[1795] Exercises and training for Norwegian personnel and units take place both nationally and in other countries, and personnel and units from other countries train and exercise in Norway

[1797] Proper drills and training are a fundamental prerequisite for maintaining and further developing the Armed Forces' operational capability, that is, the Armed Forces' ability to carry out its tasks and deliver the capabilities it is expected to contribute in various types of situations

[1798] Examples of some of the elements that are important to practice are the national command structure's ability to plan and lead joint operations (operations in which several branches of defense operate together) and the ability of national forces to interact across the branches of defense, with allied countries and with civilian actors

[1838] Protection against weapons of mass destruction CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear) weapons are an international collective term

[1935] Basic principles for the organization of the Armed Forces

[1936] Based on the goals, tasks and operational needs described in this chapter, and derived from the security policy and societal developments in the previous chapters, a number of fundamental principles for the organisation of the Armed Forces are set out here

[1937] These principles shall guide the development of the Armed Forces' structure and operational capabilities

[1938] A modern, balanced operational defense Norway needs a modern, alliance-adapted operational defense that can meet various challenges at home and abroad

[1939] Such a defense must maintain high quality and possess high competence, flexibility, responsiveness, mobility and the ability to build up forces

[1940] The Armed Forces must be capable of high-intensity combat, and in addition have the ability to provide an adapted and relevant response across the entire spectrum of conflicts

[1941] The Armed Forces' operational units must combine great firepower and self-protection with effective information gathering capabilities and the ability to disseminate and utilize information in effective networks

[1942] The Armed Forces must develop and maintain sufficient operational planning and contingency plans to be able to respond quickly and effectively when needed

[1943] A prerequisite for an alliance adapted operational defense is the maintenance of a balanced defense structure consisting of land, sea and air capabilities that can operate both independently and within an allied framework

[1944] Alliance adaptation The Armed Forces must have the ability to cooperate effectively with allied forces, both to meet challenges in Norway's immediate vicinity and to deliver significant contributions to international operations

[1945] The Armed Forces should therefore, as far as possible, be adapted to NATO standards, concepts, procedures and force structure at all levels

[1946] It is also an objective that Norway's national command and control capacity should be integrated with NATO's command structure to the greatest extent possible, and be dimensioned to meet these needs

[1947] This is central to ensuring national influence in allied operations in Norway, to facilitate the best possible reception of allied reinforcements for exercises and operations in our immediate area, and to ensure that Norway can contribute to NATO's joint operations abroad with these capacities as well

[1948] Ability for multinational cooperation The Armed Forces will continue their efforts to seek cost-effective solutions through multinational defense cooperation

[1949] It will be emphasized that such multinational cooperation provides documented economic benefits

[1950] Norway will continue to be a driving force for joint solutions within the NATO framework, but will also seek opportunities for cost-effective construction

[1951] A defense for our time is the development of prioritized capabilities through bilateral and multilateral cooperation

[1952] Follow-up and further development of Nordic defense cooperation within the framework of NORDEFCO will continue to have high priority, with a focus on mutually reinforcing measures to achieve more effective capability development

[1953] Military service and competence

[1954] The defense of Norway is based on conscription

[1955] Military service is a contract between citizens and the state that entails a joint duty to stand together to protect our society, our democratic system and our common values

[1956] Conscription helps to ensure the legitimacy of the Armed Forces and their anchoring in society

[1957] Through conscription, the Armed Forces ensure broad recruitment across social and cultural divides

[1958] The first-time service will be further developed to suit the requirements of the Norwegian Armed Forces

[1959] At the same time, the Armed Forces also need personnel who are in service beyond their initial service

[1960] Some advanced weapons systems require such extensive training that it is desirable that the operators can be available for a longer period of time than conscripts

[1961] Many international assignments require personnel who are thoroughly trained and prepared, not least to meet personnel safety requirements

[1962] In addition to the foundation provided by conscription, the Armed Forces must therefore have a component of conscripted personnel in some operational departments

[1963] The Armed Forces shall be further developed as a competence organization that can meet the challenges of the future

[1964] The Armed Forces must be able to care for personnel participating in multinational operations and their loved ones

[1965] Personnel with experience from international operations are a great resource both for the Defence Forces and for Norwegian society as a whole

[1966] At the same time, such service can be burdensome

[1967] The Defence Force must therefore emphasize both preventive measures and, in collaboration with other sectors, ensure good help and follow-up for those who may need it

[1968] The Government will further develop the work to strengthen the recognition and care of veterans in line with the Government's action plan "In service of Norway

[1969] Norway needs a defense that is flexible, robust and capable of handling various challenges

[1970] The defence structure will primarily be designed to solve the dimensioning tasks and the current challenges that can be derived from these

[1971] However, it is equally important that the Armed Forces develop the ability to respond to situations that do not, or only partially, coincide with anticipated scenarios

[1972] The Armed Forces must be able to utilize available capacities to solve a broad range of missions

[1973] The armed forces must be in continuous development and adaptation

[1974] The Armed Forces must constantly observe current international developments in the military field, both among allies, partners and potential adversaries, technologically, conceptually and doctrinally

[1975] Foresight in a defense context also implies the ability for long-term planning

[1976] It is particularly important that major and costly investments are future-oriented, and that planning for procurement, phasing in and staffing starts early enough to ensure that relevant capabilities are continued when older equipment reaches the end of its service life

[1977] Cooperation with civil authorities

[1978] The Armed Forces' cooperation with civilian actors must be further developed to ensure efficiency based on good planning and functional procedures

[1979] Well-coordinated and mutual cooperation across the entire crisis spectrum must be facilitated within the framework of total defense

[1980] Where relevant, assistance to civil society shall be taken into account when designing the Armed Forces' capabilities

[1981] Sustainability The Armed Forces shall be developed with a long-term perspective that ensures that financial resources, tasks and level of ambition are in line with each other

[1982] The capacities in which investments are made must be able to operate over time at a defined level of activity

[1983] This places high demands on the quality of the preparatory work prior to new acquisitions, and the ability to operate cost-effectively and rationally

[1984] Resources must be channeled to the greatest extent possible so that they support operational deliveries

[1985] However, it is also important that operational activities, such as contributions to international operations, do not over time reach a higher level than the force production apparatus is capable of supporting

[1986] A defense for our time

[1987] Balancing considerations

[1988] In some areas, the Armed Forces will have to balance considerations that pull in different directions

[1989] Reactivity is central to modern operational defense

[1990] The ability to respond immediately with relevant capacities is particularly important in crises that may arise in one's own home area, but international operations may also require the ability to respond quickly

[1991] Responsiveness requires capacities with availability, deployability and mobility

[1992] The transition to a response defense system from the beginning of the 2000s was based precisely on the recognition that the old invasion defense system was too cumbersome and would not be able to respond quickly enough in crises either at home or abroad

[1993] At the same time, modern operational defense also needs the ability to build up forces and a certain amount of endurance

[1994] Not least, many international operations have proven to require forces that can withstand the test of time

[1995] The ability to endure is ensured not only by having available forces, but equally through efficient logistics and a well-functioning support concept

[1996] Quality is also central to modern operational defense

[1997] Experience shows that modern capabilities can combat units that are larger in volume but weaker in quality

[1998] Norway's comparative advantage, at home as well as abroad, lies in expertise and technology, rather than in the ability to field numerically large units

[1999] Norway must therefore prioritize quality – units where efficiency, mobility and firepower are high compared to the number of personnel

[2000] At the same time, a certain volume is a prerequisite for ensuring the necessary robustness and flexibility

[2001] Volume is also closely linked to endurance

[2002] By reducing the breadth of capabilities, a defense structure can achieve greater depth and quality within a limited range of capabilities

[2003] Such a niche strategy also results in increased dependence on allies, who, if necessary, must contribute key capacities that are not available in their own structure

[2004] The Norwegian Armed Forces have a number of tasks that are initially designed to be solved with national capabilities

[2005] In addition, a certain breadth of capabilities is required if the Armed Forces' war prevention function is to appear credible

[2006] Consequently, a significant reduction in capacity width is not a current strategy for Norway

[2007] Norwegian forces must carry out tasks both at home and abroad

[2008] The defense of Norway will always be the most important task of the Armed Forces

[2009] At the same time, it is in Norway's interest to contribute to international peace and stability through participation in international operations

[2010] Such contributions demonstrate Norway's ability and willingness to meet its obligations, show international solidarity and contribute to burden sharing

[2011] Contributions to international operations also have practical benefits that are of great relevance to Norwegian security

[2012] Through international operations, the Armed Forces are provided with valuable expertise and experience

[2013] Among other things, through international operations, the Armed Forces have gained increased experience in collaborating with others in demanding integrated operations

[2014] The operations also provide an opportunity to demonstrate skills and combat capability

[2015] All of this strengthens the credibility of the Armed Forces, also in a domestic context

[2016] The Armed Forces' capabilities should therefore be developed to the greatest extent possible so that they can be used both nationally and in international operations

[2017] Even if units for international operations are tailored for the purpose, extensive investment in mission-specific capabilities that cannot be expected to have relevance beyond the operation in question should be avoided as far as possible

[2018] Considerations for force protection may nevertheless make it necessary to deviate from such a general rule

[2019] Contributions to international operations not only involve increased expertise, but also place a burden on the Armed Forces, primarily on the departments that participate

[2020] These burdens increase if the assignments persist over time, if the scope for longer periods exceeds the level of ambition in current plans, or if certain environments are continuously imposed with more extensive contributions than they are designed for

[2021] It is therefore important that international operations are used consciously so that they help build, rather than erode, operational capability

[2022] To avoid skewing

[2023] distribution of both burdens and competence gains, efforts will be made to spread contributions to international operations between branches of defence and units where possible

[2024] Mutually reinforcing competence building and synergy must characterize the relationship between home and outdoor tasks

[2025] Concurrency issues concern the ability to handle multiple challenges that coincide in time

[2026] Even though the Armed Forces are engaged in international operations, they must have the ability to handle national tasks – both ongoing routine peacetime tasks and rapidly emerging crises

[2027] The armed forces must therefore be developed with an appropriate balance between responsiveness, endurance and volume, so that Norway can make a significant contribution to international operations while at the same time maintaining a satisfactory ability for effective national crisis management in its own immediate areas

[2028] The scope of the capabilities that must be maintained in Norway at all times in areas such as command and control. 2011–2012 Prop

[2029] A defense for our time - trolls, surveillance and intelligence, the exercise of authority, assertion of sovereignty, crisis management and societal security - must be based on an ongoing overall assessment of the security political situation in the surrounding areas and the need for contributions to ongoing international operations

[2030] In the event of prolonged serious national crisis situations, it may be appropriate to withdraw one's own forces from international operations, but the ability to handle challenges that require rapid reaction cannot be based on this

[2104] New combat aircraft for the Armed Forces

[2105] This is what the F-35 adds to the Armed Forces

[2106] When Norway acquired the F-16, the aircraft's mission was primarily to defend Norwegian airspace

[2107] In the 1980s, the need arose to also be able to neutralize targets on the ground or on the sea surface

[2108] Investments were made in new weapons and the F-16 was upgraded to meet this need

[2109] In the 1990s, neutralizing targets on the ground became even more important, and greater demands were placed on aircraft to also be able to deliver precision-delivered weapons against ground targets

[2110] With the implementation of the Mid-Life Update (MLU), weapons investments and further upgrades, the F-16 has evolved over a period of 30 years from a fighter aircraft for the air defense role to a multi-role combat aircraft

[2111] The F-16 is nearing the end of its service life

[2112] In 2009, through the consideration of Recommendation

[2113] no. 299 (2008– 2009), cf. St.prp

[2114] No. 36 (2008–2009) New combat aircraft for the Armed Forces, the Storting agreed that the F-35 should replace the F-16 as the backbone of the Air Force and the Defence Forces for the next 40 years

[2115] Fighter aircraft are a fundamental capability in our defense structure

[2116] Modern combat aircraft are a prerequisite for maintaining the Armed Forces' ability to react quickly over long distances

[2117] No other weapon can protect one's own forces, population and areas against air attacks in the same way

[2118] Fighter aircraft are a prerequisite for enforcing Norwegian sovereignty- 2011–

[2119] A defense for our time in the airspace, in peace, crisis and war

[2120] A modern combat aircraft is an absolutely necessary part of a war prevention threshold

[2121] Since combat aircraft are a capability that is very difficult for an attacker to circumvent or render irrelevant, even a technologically advanced adversary will not be able to ignore the resistance that a modern combat aircraft can provide

[2122] By creating great uncertainty among an adversary about the possible consequences of aggression against Norway, the aircraft have a significant deterrent effect

[2123] Rapid technological development increases the possibilities for new high-tech weapons and sensors to be developed, and for existing weapons to be improved with advanced control systems or other additional equipment

[2124] This opens up new perspectives on warfare that we must be prepared to face

[2125] In the future, our fighter aircraft must have the ability to operate effectively in such a modern combat environment, and have the ability for advanced operations or the range to inflict losses on the enemy from a safe distance

[2126] The combat air force must be prepared for the means the opponent may use, and capable of using the same range of means itself

[2127] Consequently, a modern combat aircraft must be a flexible capability that can both strike the enemy and at the same time protect its own ability to operate in the entire combat environment

[2128] The threat landscape of the future will present different challenges than today

[2129] The greatest perceived threat to fighter aircraft as a system is enemy fighter aircraft, surface-to-air missiles and other air defenses

[2130] Electronic warfare is also a threat, and resilience to this is essential

[2131] Several of the leading fighter aircraft manufacturers emphasize low radar signature in their development projects, including the USA, Russia and China

[2132] The F-35 has a low radar signature as a result of both the aircraft's unique design and the choice of materials on its external surfaces

[2133] The F-35, with its all-weather capability, unique sensors and advanced weapons, combined with advanced communications technology, will be a hub in future network-based joint operations

[2134] The fighter's ability to interact with other systems strengthens the joint operational capability and is crucial for the Armed Forces to be able to handle the most demanding tasks

[2135] A network-based defense, including fighter aircraft and frigates, will be able to extract increased effectiveness from both structural elements and achieve major synergy effects during land and sea operations

[2136] To achieve synergy effects with other Norwegian forces, Norway needs a combat air force of sufficient size, capable of both establishing air control in time and space and at the same time carrying out offensive operations in support of land and sea operations

[2137] The ability to ensure air control in time and space is crucial for the protection of our own land and naval forces, as well as being able to prepare the conditions for the reception of allied reinforcements

[2138] Modern combat aircraft are crucial for handling air forces and air defenses that an adversary uses to deny Norwegian air operations over the operational area

[2139] An opponent without air control will be similarly vulnerable to attack from the air

[2140] By having the ability to control the air, such a vulnerability can be exploited and thus give one's own forces great advantages in the sea, land and air domains

[2141] The aircraft's capabilities in air-to-ground operations will provide the opportunity for direct and indirect support to ground forces and contribute to more effective land operations

[2142] This also applies to direct fire support under the direction of Forward Air Controllers (FAC

[2143] The aircraft contributes to increased situational awareness through sensors and mobility, extended range for integrated communications and information systems, and the ability to deliver long-range precision fire, both as an independent element and in support of land and sea elements

[2144] The acquisition of new fighter aircraft does not only mean that the current fighter aircraft capacity is continued by replacing an aging fighter fleet with a new one

[2145] The F-35 will provide the Norwegian Armed Forces with a significantly enhanced capability, not only for the combat air force in isolation, but for the entire Norwegian Armed Forces

[2146] The acquisition involves both a strictly necessary renewal of an important component in our overall defense structure and a significant improvement in the overall combat effectiveness of the Armed Forces

[2147] Alignment of the future air defense In the St.prop

[2148] No. 48 (2007–2008), the government pointed out that the base and support structure “is still characterized by a legacy that represents a costly dispersion of activities

[2149] …] In the future, the Air Force should continue to expand the breadth of its capabilities, but concentrated on fewer bases, with the premise that similar professional environments are co-located where it is rational.”

[2150] The acquisition of new combat aircraft with the associated need for updating the base and support structure will, in this context, serve as a catalyst for Prop

[2151] A defense for our time is a necessary reform of the Air Force's base and support structure in general

[2152] The structure of the Air Force reflects a historical legacy and is largely based on operational needs that are not to the same extent current

[2153] The introduction of new combat aircraft makes it both desirable and necessary to look at the overall structure of the Air Force and implement measures to streamline and modernize it

[2154] The F-35 development program

[2155] The basic idea behind the multinational F-35 program was the development and production of an aircraft that, with its multi-role capability, could replace a number of current aircraft types

[2156] Parallel development and testing, combined with production of a large number of aircraft, should result in a short development phase and lower unit cost

[2157] This is a demanding goal and a high ambition for an aircraft development program

[2158] Despite challenges in the development of the aircraft and restructuring of the production and development processes, the program can now show good results in terms of both expected performance and price

[2159] The multinational program has followed the revised development plan for the past year with only minor deviations

[2160] The Norwegian procurement has been subject to continuous assessment in parallel with the development of the F-35 program, and in the fall of 2010 the Norwegian delivery plan was adjusted and adapted to the updated development plan

[2161] Today, the biggest challenge for the program is the international financial situation, which has caused several nations, for budgetary reasons, to adjust their procurement plans and procure a somewhat lower number of aircraft later than planned

[2162] At the same time, the F-35 program is the only Western fifth-generation multirole fighter aircraft under development

[2163] Many nations are now planning to replace their third- and fourth-generation fighter aircraft

[2164] Nine partner countries participate in the multinational F-35 program, procuring an aircraft capable of meeting the challenges of the future

[2165] There is therefore still strong support for the program among the partner nations

[2166] In addition, there are several new countries that have decided, or are planning, to acquire the F

[2167] Overall, a total production of more than 3,000 aircraft in three versions is still planned

[2204] The overall dimensioning of the combat air force is based on two fundamental assumptions

[2207] Furthermore, it is assumed that the combat air force should be able to support naval forces and land forces, without having to be removed from air defense tasks

[2208] This is because Norway's air defenses have not been developed with the aim of maintaining control in the air without fighter aircraft being the core capacity in such a mission

[2246] Implementation of the acquisition Combat aircraft are a fundamental capability in the Norwegian Armed Forces and have a major impact on the Norwegian Armed Forces' overall capability

[2247] At the same time, the new fighter jets are a very costly capability that, if fully covered within the current defense framework, would have to entail significant reductions in the rest of the structure, and a corresponding reduction in the ability to fulfill the defense ambition

[2248] Continuing the tasks and level of ambition requires a fighter aircraft capacity in line with the level of ambition that has been set

[2249] Continuing a defense structure that is capable of maintaining the mission focus and level of ambition will therefore require a temporary increase in the defense framework

[2250] As a basic prerequisite for the acquisition of fighter aircraft, the government is therefore planning a temporary, but significant, strengthening of the defense framework to cover the costs of acquiring fighter aircraft and the associated basing solution

[2251] The government has faced several dilemmas here

[2252] On the one hand, there is a need to secure one of the defense structure's most important capabilities for the future

[2253] On the other hand, this replacement is so costly that it could take up significant parts of the financial room for manoeuvre in the state budget in the years to come

[2254] Alternatively, a larger part of the costs of the acquisition must be covered within the ordinary defense framework, with associated consequences for other parts of the Armed Forces

[2255] It is challenging to find the right balance between a new combat aircraft, space within the ordinary defense framework and necessary increases in defense spending to cover the acquisition, set against the expected future room for maneuver in the state budget

[2256] The Government believes that these various trade-offs have been taken into account through the comprehensive proposal presented in this bill

[2316] Organization of the new combat air force The organization of the new combat air force must reflect the fact that the Air Force is a competence-intensive and technology-driven organization

[2317] A fighter aircraft organization consisting of two squadrons located at the main base on Ørland is planned

[2318] In addition to the squadron pilots, a smaller number of pilots are planned to fill functions in central organizations, staffs at air stations, headquarters and inspectorates for direct support of combat aircraft functions

[2319] Further plans include an adapted operational support organization to support combat aircraft operations

[2320] Operational and technical training The operational training concept for the F-35 describes a training course for F-35 fighter pilots from the completion of basic pilot training until they achieve combat-ready status at the squadron

[2321] First, basic combat training is conducted before starting training on the F-35 at a multinational pilot training center in the United States

[2322] Upon returning to Norway, all pilots must complete an adapted Norwegian qualification program

[2323] After completing the qualification program, the pilots will serve at the squadron and in subsequent service will maintain their qualifications through an annual training program adapted to Norwegian conditions and the roles for which Norwegian combat pilots must be qualified

[2324] As much of the annual training as possible will be conducted in advanced F-35 simulators linked together in a network

[2325] The simulator concept helps pilots get a better effect from the training carried out in the aircraft and allows pilots to train in conditions that cannot be carried out in the aircraft due to safety reasons

[2326] Simulator training will be carried out to a significantly greater extent than today

[2327] During the transition from F-16 to F-35, there will be a period of need to convert Norwegian F-16 pilots to the F-35 aircraft type

[2328] These pilots will undergo a customized course at the multinational pilot training center in the United States, so that they can return to Norway as quickly as possible and contribute to building operational capacity in Norway

[2329] The training of maintenance personnel will be adapted to the Norwegian maintenance concept and the basic competence level of Norwegian technicians

[2330] The F-35 type training can be carried out in two different ways

[2331] conversion course for already serving and certified personnel, and an educational course for newly qualified technicians

[2332] Conversion training for Norwegian personnel is planned to be started at a multinational training center in the United States during
